lessons.title: Root System: Parts and Jobs
lessons.notes_html:
A plant has two systems: the root system below the ground and the shoot system above the ground. The root system absorbs water and nutrients from the soil.

Parts of the Root System

  • Primary root (tap root) — grows downwards from the radicle of the embryo.
  • Secondary roots — smaller roots growing from the primary root.
  • Tertiary roots — further branches of secondary roots.
  • Grasses and strawberry have threadlike fibrous roots spread in the soil, not growing deep.

Tip of the Root

  • Root meristem — rapidly dividing cells at the tip.
  • Root cap — covers and protects the meristem.
  • Root hairs — tiny hair-like outgrowths of the epidermis. They increase the surface area for absorption of water and nutrients.

The root has three regions: region of meristematic activity, region of elongation and region of maturation. The cortex in roots also stores food.

Key Points

  • Root hairs increase surface area for absorption.
  • The root cap protects the growing tip.

mcqs.q: Which plant system grows below the ground?
mcqs.why: A plant has two systems: the root system below the ground and the shoot system above the ground.

mcqs.q: What is the main job of the root system?
options: To absorb water and nutrients from the soil
To support the leaves in sunlight
mcqs.why: The root system absorbs water and nutrients from the soil, while food-making is the work of the leaves.

mcqs.why: The primary root (tap root) grows downwards from the radicle of the embryo.

mcqs.q: Smaller roots that grow out of the primary root are called:
mcqs.why: Secondary roots are the smaller roots growing from the primary root; tertiary roots are further branches of the secondary roots.

mcqs.q: Grasses and strawberry plants have which kind of roots?
options: Threadlike fibrous roots spread in the soil
Roots with a thick root cap only
mcqs.why: Grasses and strawberry have threadlike fibrous roots spread in the soil, not growing deep.

options: It absorbs water from the soil

It divides rapidly to make new cells

mcqs.why: The root cap covers and protects the meristem, the region of rapidly dividing cells at the root tip.

options: Increase the surface area for absorbing water and nutrients
Push the root deeper into the soil

mcqs.why: Root hairs are tiny outgrowths of the epidermis that increase the surface area for absorption of water and nutrients.

mcqs.why: The root has three regions: region of meristematic activity, region of elongation and region of maturation.

mcqs.why: The notes state that the cortex in roots also stores food.

mcqs.why: The root meristem is the region of rapidly dividing cells at the tip, protected by the root cap.

lessons.title: Inside the Root and Stem
lessons.notes_html:
Root and stem look different outside, and their inner tissues are arranged differently too.

Inside the Root

  • Epidermis — outermost layer with root hairs; protects inner cells and absorbs water and nutrients.
  • Cortex — many layers of thin-walled round cells; carries absorbed water to the vascular bundles and stores reserve food.
  • Endodermis — innermost layer of the cortex, of barrel-shaped cells; regulates movement of water and hormones into and out of the vascular bundles.
  • Vascular bundles — xylem and phloem, with the pericycle between endodermis and bundles.

Inside the Stem

  • Epidermis — outer layer coated with a wax-like cuticle; prevents water loss and mechanical injury.
  • Cortex — supports the stem and stores food.
  • Vascular bundles — tubular xylem and phloem transporting water, minerals and food.
  • Cambium — produces new vascular tissues, so the stem grows in diameter.
  • Pith — central parenchyma cells storing nutrients and giving support.
FeatureRootStem
Outer layerRoot hairs presentCuticle present
Special layersEndodermis and pericycleCambium and central pith

Key Points

  • Epidermis is outermost; endodermis is innermost cortex layer.
  • Cambium makes the stem thicker; the root has no pith or cambium.

mcqs.why: The epidermis is the outermost layer of the root; it has root hairs, protects inner cells and absorbs water and nutrients.

mcqs.q: The cortex of a root is made of:
options: A single layer of barrel-shaped cells
Many layers of thin-walled round cells
mcqs.why: The cortex consists of many layers of thin-walled round cells that carry absorbed water to the vascular bundles and store reserve food.

mcqs.why: The endodermis is the innermost layer of the cortex, made of barrel-shaped cells.

options: Movement of water and hormones into and out of the vascular bundles
mcqs.why: The endodermis regulates movement of water and hormones into and out of the vascular bundles.

mcqs.why: The stem epidermis is coated with a wax-like cuticle which prevents water loss and mechanical injury.

mcqs.why: Cambium produces new vascular tissues, so the stem grows in diameter.

mcqs.why: The pith is the central parenchyma of the stem; it stores nutrients and gives support.

mcqs.q: A root differs from a stem because the root has:
mcqs.why: The comparison table shows the root's special layers are endodermis and pericycle, while the stem has cambium and central pith.

options: Between the endodermis and the vascular bundles
In the centre of the pith
mcqs.why: The notes place the pericycle between the endodermis and the vascular bundles in the root.

mcqs.q: According to the notes, the root has no:
mcqs.why: The key points state: cambium makes the stem thicker; the root has no pith or cambium.

lessons.title: Shoot System and Vascular Tissues
lessons.notes_html:
The shoot system is made of stem, leaves, flowers and fruit — all the above-ground parts.

Jobs of the Shoot System

  • Conducts water from roots to leaves for making food.
  • Supports leaves and branches — the stem supports all other shoot parts.
  • Transports food to every part of the plant body.
  • Leaves are the main site of photosynthesis, gaseous exchange and removal of extra water.

The stem bears nodes (where a leaf is attached) and internodes (the part between two nodes).

Xylem and Phloem

FeatureXylemPhloem
CarriesWater and nutrients from roots to leavesFood from leaves to other parts
Position in stemTowards the centreCloser to the outer edge
FlowOne-wayTwo-way
WallsThick, stiffened with lignin; no end wallsTubular living tissue

Together xylem and phloem form the vascular bundles.

Key Points

  • Xylem carries water upwards; phloem carries food.
  • Vascular bundles consist of xylem and phloem.

mcqs.q: The shoot system of a plant is made of:
options: Roots, root hairs and root cap
mcqs.why: The shoot system is made of stem, leaves, flowers and fruit — all the above-ground parts of the plant.

mcqs.q: Which part of the shoot system supports all the other shoot parts?
mcqs.why: The stem supports leaves and branches — it supports all other shoot parts.

mcqs.q: Leaves are the main site of:
options: Photosynthesis, gaseous exchange and removal of extra water
mcqs.why: The notes list leaves as the main site of photosynthesis, gaseous exchange and removal of extra water.

mcqs.q: The part of the stem where a leaf is attached is called a:
mcqs.why: The stem bears nodes (where a leaf is attached) and internodes (the part between two nodes).

mcqs.q: Xylem carries:
options: Water and nutrients from roots to leaves
Food from leaves to other parts
Water from leaves down to roots
mcqs.why: Xylem carries water and nutrients from roots to leaves; phloem carries food from leaves to other parts.

mcqs.why: The comparison table places xylem towards the centre and phloem closer to the outer edge of the stem.

mcqs.why: Xylem flow is one-way, while phloem flow is two-way, as food moves to wherever it is needed or stored.

options: Thin and full of living cytoplasm
Thick, stiffened with lignin, with no end walls
mcqs.why: Xylem has thick walls stiffened with lignin and no end walls; phloem is tubular living tissue.

mcqs.why: Together xylem and phloem form the vascular bundles of the plant.

options: Absorb minerals directly from the air
Conduct water from roots to leaves for making food
mcqs.why: The shoot system conducts water from roots to leaves for making food and transports food to every part of the plant body.

lessons.title: Inside the Leaf and Photosynthesis
lessons.notes_html:
Leaves make food by photosynthesis: plants prepare their own food using water and carbon dioxide in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll.

Equation: Carbon dioxide + Water → (Sunlight, Chlorophyll) Food (Glucose) + Oxygen. Besides oxygen, the main product is glucose.

Inside the Leaf

  • Upper epidermis — protective layer with cuticle; conserves water.
  • Palisade mesophyll — just below upper epidermis; regularly arranged elongated cells rich in chloroplasts; main site of photosynthesis.
  • Spongy mesophyll — near lower epidermis; irregular cells with air spaces for exchange of gases.
  • Vascular bundles (veins) — xylem supplies water and minerals; phloem transports food.
  • Lower epidermis — has pores called stomata for gas exchange and removal of extra water; each stoma has two guard cells controlling opening and closing.

How the Leaf Suits Photosynthesis

  • Broad and flat — large surface area for sunlight.
  • Thin, transparent epidermis — lets sunlight reach deeper cells.
  • Chloroplasts with green chlorophyll capture sunlight; magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll and nitrogen to make proteins.
  • Stomata let carbon dioxide in and oxygen out.
  • Veins spread through the leaf to supply water and carry food away.

Key Points

  • Chlorophyll is green; photosynthesis makes glucose and oxygen.
  • Palisade cells do most photosynthesis; spongy cells exchange gases.

mcqs.q: Photosynthesis is the process in which plants:
options: Release energy by breaking down glucose
Prepare their own food using water and carbon dioxide in sunlight
mcqs.why: In photosynthesis plants prepare their own food using water and carbon dioxide in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll.

mcqs.q: Besides glucose, the other product of photosynthesis is:
mcqs.why: The photosynthesis equation is: carbon dioxide + water → (sunlight, chlorophyll) food (glucose) + oxygen.

mcqs.q: Which layer of the leaf is the main site of photosynthesis?
mcqs.why: Palisade mesophyll cells, just below the upper epidermis, are rich in chloroplasts and are the main site of photosynthesis.

mcqs.q: The spongy mesophyll helps the leaf by:
options: Having air spaces for exchange of gases
mcqs.why: Spongy mesophyll, near the lower epidermis, has irregular cells with air spaces for exchange of gases.

mcqs.q: Stomata are found on the:
mcqs.why: The lower epidermis has pores called stomata for gas exchange and removal of extra water.

mcqs.q: Each stoma is controlled by:
mcqs.why: Each stoma has two guard cells controlling its opening and closing.

mcqs.q: A leaf is broad and flat so that it has:
options: A large surface area for sunlight
mcqs.why: A broad, flat leaf gives a large surface area to capture sunlight for photosynthesis.

mcqs.q: Which element is needed to make chlorophyll?
mcqs.why: The notes state magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll and nitrogen to make proteins.

mcqs.q: In the leaf veins, phloem does the job of:
mcqs.why: In vascular bundles (veins), xylem supplies water and minerals while phloem transports food.

mcqs.q: The thin, transparent epidermis of the leaf helps photosynthesis because it:
options: Lets sunlight reach the deeper cells
mcqs.why: A thin, transparent epidermis lets sunlight reach deeper cells where the chloroplasts are.

lessons.title: Respiration, Transpiration and Rise of Water
lessons.notes_html:
Respiration is the process of releasing energy: Food (Glucose) + Oxygen → Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy (ATP). Its reactants are glucose and oxygen; its products are carbon dioxide, water and energy.

FeaturePhotosynthesisRespiration
WhereChloroplasts; green plants, algae, some bacteriaMitochondria; all living organisms
EnergyUses sunlight to prepare foodReleases energy from food
GasesTakes in carbon dioxide, gives out oxygenTakes in oxygen, gives out carbon dioxide

Transpiration

Transpiration is the loss of water vapour, mostly from leaves — like a plant sweating. When stomata open for carbon dioxide, water vapour escapes. Factors: higher temperature, wind and light intensity increase the rate; higher humidity decreases it.

How Water Rises — the Plant's Own Pump

  • Evaporation from leaves creates a pull, like sucking through a straw.
  • Cohesion — water molecules attract each other, so water moves up in a continuous column.
  • Adhesion — water sticks to xylem walls; liquids rise in narrow tubes by this force.

Uses: carries dissolved nutrients up, cools the plant, keeps a constant water supply for photosynthesis, helps uptake of minerals and keeps cells firm by turgor pressure.

Key Points

  • Respiration releases energy; transpiration loses water vapour.
  • Cohesion and adhesion together raise water to the leaves.

mcqs.q: Respiration is the process of:
mcqs.why: Respiration releases energy: food (glucose) + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy (ATP).

mcqs.q: The products of respiration are:
mcqs.why: Respiration breaks down glucose with oxygen and produces carbon dioxide, water and energy (ATP).

mcqs.q: Respiration takes place in the:
mcqs.why: The comparison table shows respiration occurs in mitochondria and takes place in all living organisms.

mcqs.q: Transpiration is:
options: The making of food in leaves
The absorption of water by roots
The loss of water vapour, mostly from leaves
mcqs.why: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour, mostly from leaves — like a plant sweating.

mcqs.q: Which factor DECREASES the rate of transpiration?
mcqs.why: Higher temperature, wind and light intensity increase transpiration rate; higher humidity decreases it.

mcqs.q: In the rise of water, cohesion means:
options: Water sticks to the xylem walls
Water molecules attract each other, forming a continuous column
Water is absorbed by root hairs
mcqs.why: Cohesion is the attraction between water molecules, so water moves up in a continuous column; adhesion is sticking to xylem walls.

mcqs.q: Adhesion helps water rise because:
options: Water sticks to the xylem walls in narrow tubes
mcqs.why: Adhesion is the sticking of water to xylem walls; liquids rise in narrow tubes by this force.

mcqs.q: The pull that starts the rise of water in a plant is created by:
options: Evaporation of water from the leaves
mcqs.why: Evaporation from leaves creates a pull, like sucking through a straw, which draws water up the xylem.

mcqs.q: Transpiration helps the plant by:
options: Cooling the plant and carrying dissolved nutrients up
mcqs.why: Transpiration carries dissolved nutrients up, cools the plant, keeps a constant water supply for photosynthesis and helps uptake of minerals.

mcqs.q: Turgor pressure in cells, helped by water supply, keeps the cells:
mcqs.why: The notes say the water supply keeps cells firm by turgor pressure.

lessons.title: Breathing and the Path of Air
lessons.notes_html:
Breathing takes place in the lungs: inhaling oxygen and exhaling carbon dioxide. It produces no energy — it brings oxygen in and removes carbon dioxide, and is controlled by the brain.

Path of Air

  • Nose and nostrils — hair and mucus keep air clean, moist and warm.
  • Throat and larynx — has two vocal cords that produce sound. The epiglottis covers the breathing tube when food enters the oesophagus, so food does not enter the breathing tube. It controls the entrance of food and air into the relevant tubes.
  • Trachea — rings of cartilage keep the tube open.
  • Bronchi — two tubes, one entering each lung.
  • Bronchioles — smaller dividing tubes.
  • Alveoli — tiny air sacs where gas exchange takes place.

Mechanism of Breathing

  • Inhaling: rib muscles contract, ribs push outward, chest expands, the dome-like diaphragm flattens, cavity volume increases and air enters the lungs.
  • Exhaling: the reverse — ribs and diaphragm return, volume decreases, chest contracts and air is expelled.

Key Points

  • The epiglottis guards the windpipe during swallowing.
  • Gas exchange happens in the alveoli, not in the trachea or bronchi.

options: Produces no energy — it only brings oxygen in and removes carbon dioxide
mcqs.why: Breathing takes place in the lungs and produces no energy; it brings oxygen in and removes carbon dioxide and is controlled by the brain.

mcqs.why: In the nose and nostrils, hair and mucus keep air clean, moist and warm.

mcqs.why: The throat and larynx have two vocal cords that produce sound.

mcqs.why: The epiglottis covers the breathing tube when food enters the oesophagus, so food does not enter the breathing tube.

mcqs.q: The trachea is kept open by:
mcqs.why: The trachea has rings of cartilage that keep the tube open.

mcqs.why: Bronchi are two tubes, one entering each lung; they divide into smaller bronchioles ending in alveoli.

mcqs.why: Alveoli are tiny air sacs where gas exchange takes place — not in the trachea or bronchi.

lessons.title: Respiration in Cells: Aerobic and Anaerobic
lessons.notes_html:
Respiration is a biochemical process in every cell in which oxygen reacts with food (glucose) to release energy as ATP (adenosine triphosphate). Each reaction is helped by a specific enzyme.

FeatureAerobic respirationAnaerobic respiration
OxygenPresentAbsent
Place in cellMitochondriaMostly cytoplasm
EnergyMore energyLess energy
ByproductsCarbon dioxide and waterIn yeast: alcohol and carbon dioxide; in muscles: lactic acid

Anaerobic Respiration in Our Body

It is like a backup plan. During intense exercise muscles cannot get enough oxygen, so food breaks down without oxygen and lactic acid forms. The lactic acid is carried to the liver, which converts it back into glucose.

Key Points

  • Aerobic respiration needs oxygen and occurs in mitochondria.
  • Anaerobic respiration in yeast gives alcohol and carbon dioxide (fermentation).

mcqs.why: Respiration is a biochemical process in every cell in which oxygen reacts with glucose to release energy as ATP.

lessons.title: The Heart: Structure and Working
lessons.notes_html:
The heart is a muscular organ about the size of one's fist, on the left side of the chest, enclosed in a membrane called the pericardium. It works like a pump — in fact a double pump.

Four Chambers

FeatureAtriaVentricles
PositionUpper two chambersLower two chambers
Size and wallsSmaller; thin wallsLarger; thicker walls
Job when pumpingPush blood into ventriclesPush blood to all body parts / lungs

Each atrium opens into its own ventricle. When the atria contract, blood enters the ventricles but cannot flow back.

Heartbeat and Pulse

  • Heartbeat is the contraction and relaxation of heart muscles.
  • A healthy person has 72–80 beats per minute at rest.
  • The heartbeat is also called the pulse, felt below the base of the thumb on the underside of the wrist.
  • During exercise the heartbeat increases because muscles need more oxygen and energy, so the heart beats faster to deliver oxygen-rich blood.

Key Points

  • Atria receive and pass blood; ventricles pump it out strongly.
  • The heart pushes oxygenated blood to the body and deoxygenated blood to the lungs.

lessons.title: Blood and Its Components
lessons.notes_html:
Blood is a vital fluid (connective tissue) that delivers essential substances and removes wastes. The circulatory system — heart, arteries and veins — carries it through the body.

ComponentJob
Red blood cells (RBCs)Most abundant cells; contain haemoglobin which binds oxygen in the lungs and carries it to tissues; give blood its red colour; carry carbon dioxide back to the lungs
White blood cells (WBCs)Cells of the immune system; protect against bacteria, viruses and fungi; act in inflammation and allergic reactions
PlateletsSmall cell fragments; clot blood to stop bleeding; release growth factors for tissue repair
PlasmaLiquid part, about 55% of blood volume; mostly water with proteins, electrolytes, hormones, nutrients, wastes and gases; helps maintain blood pressure and body temperature

Oxygenated and Deoxygenated Blood

  • Oxygenated blood — oxygen-rich; comes from the lungs; the left ventricle pushes it into the aorta to all body parts.
  • Deoxygenated blood — oxygen-poor; pushed towards the lungs.
  • Blood oxygenates in the lungs: oxygen diffuses across the thin alveoli walls into blood capillaries.

Key Points

  • Haemoglobin in RBCs carries oxygen.
  • Plasma is the liquid part — about 55% of blood.

mcqs.q: Haemoglobin is found in:

lessons.title: Arteries, Veins and Capillaries
lessons.notes_html:
Three kinds of vessels carry blood around the body.

FeatureArteriesVeinsCapillaries
DirectionHeart to body partsBody parts back to heartConnect arteries to veins
WallsThick, muscular, elastic — withstand high pressureThinner than arteries; have valvesThinnest — one layer of endothelial cells; narrowest vessels
Special pointLargest is the aortaLargest are superior and inferior vena cavae; valves stop backflowExchange of gases, food and wastes with tissues happens here

Two Exceptions to Remember

  • Pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.
  • Pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium. All other veins carry deoxygenated blood.

Capillaries and Alveoli

Do not mix them: capillaries are blood vessels where materials exchange between blood and tissues; alveoli are air sacs in the lungs where gases exchange between air and blood, surrounded by capillaries.

Key Points

  • Arteries carry blood away; veins bring it back; capillaries exchange materials.
  • Blood reaches the heart from the lungs through pulmonary veins.

options: From body parts back to the heart
From the heart to body parts
mcqs.why: Arteries carry blood from the heart to body parts; veins bring it back to the heart.

mcqs.why: Veins have thinner walls than arteries and have valves that stop backflow of blood.

mcqs.q: Exchange of gases, food and wastes with tissues happens in the:
mcqs.why: Capillaries are the thinnest vessels — one layer of endothelial cells — and exchange of gases, food and wastes with tissues happens there.

mcqs.q: The largest artery in the body is the:
mcqs.why: The largest artery is the aorta; the largest veins are the superior and inferior vena cavae.

Deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs

mcqs.q: Pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood from the lungs to the:
mcqs.why: Pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium; all other veins carry deoxygenated blood.

mcqs.q: Arterial walls are thick, muscular and elastic so they can:
mcqs.why: Arteries have thick, muscular, elastic walls to withstand the high pressure of blood pumped from the heart.

mcqs.q: Capillaries connect:
mcqs.why: Capillaries connect arteries to veins and are the narrowest vessels.

lessons.title: Immunity, Infection, Antigens and Antibodies
lessons.notes_html:
Immunity is the natural ability of the body to fight against diseases and keep us safe. When immunity against a disease becomes weak, its pathogens may attack us.

  • Infection — the entry and growth of microorganisms (pathogens) into the body of another organism. The air we breathe, the water we drink and the food we eat are not free of microorganisms.
  • Antigens — foreign substances that enter the body: pathogens like viruses, bacteria and fungi, as well as allergens and toxins.
  • Antibodies — proteins that protect the body: they identify pathogens for destruction by other immune cells and prevent them from infecting body cells.

The immune system responds to antigens by producing antibodies.

Key Points

  • Immunity fights disease; infection is the entry and growth of pathogens.
  • Antigens are foreign; antibodies are our protective proteins.

lessons.title: Three Lines of Defence
lessons.notes_html:
The body defends itself in three lines.

First Line — Barriers

Physical and chemical barriers like the skin and mucous membranes stop pathogens entering. Salivary glands in the walls of the oral cavity secrete saliva, which is antiseptic.

Second Line — Innate Response

  • When tissues are damaged by an invader, they release chemicals called cytokines.
  • Cytokines cause inflammation — burning effect, redness, swelling and pain.
  • Special inflammatory cells reach the area through blood flow to fight pathogens and promote tissue repair. Phagocytes and natural killer cells also act here.

Third Line — Adaptive Response

  • Specific and targeted; develops after exposure to specific pathogens or antigens.
  • Uses T-lymphocytes and B-lymphocytes and forms memory cells, giving long-term protection: on re-exposure the response is rapid and effective.
  • Lymphocytes are the white blood cells that develop this defence system.

Key Points

  • Barriers first, inflammation second, lymphocytes and memory third.
  • Cytokines trigger inflammation.

lessons.title: Vaccines, Strong Immunity and Staying Safe
lessons.notes_html:
A vaccine is a preparation of dead or weak pathogens of a disease injected into the body to produce active immunity — the body then produces its own antibodies, which takes time. Do not confuse it with cytokines, the chemicals released by damaged tissues that cause inflammation.

T-cells and B-cells

  • B-lymphocytes — associated with production of antibodies.
  • T-lymphocytes — directly recognise and destroy infected cells and coordinate the adaptive response.

Strengthening Immunity

  • Healthy diet — balanced diet with fruits, vegetables, whole grains, lean proteins and healthy fats.
  • Regular exercise — walking, jogging, cycling or sports; boosts blood circulation, promotes immune cells and reduces stress.
  • Also: staying hydrated and sufficient sleep.

Safeguards Against Infectious Diseases

  • Masks — barrier against respiratory droplets carrying viruses or bacteria (COVID-19, flu).
  • Hand washing — 20 seconds with soap and water; sanitizers also kill germs.
  • Also: physical distancing (at least 1 metre / 3 feet), respiratory etiquette, vaccination, and cleaning frequently touched surfaces.

Hepatitis and COVID-19

  • Hepatitis — viruses A, B, C, D, E infect the liver; spread by contaminated food/water or infected blood; diagnosed by blood tests; prevented by vaccination (A and B), hygiene and safe food and water.
  • COVID-19 — caused by SARS-CoV-2; spreads by respiratory droplets and contaminated surfaces; diagnosed by PCR test (and rapid antigen tests); prevented by masks, distancing, hand washing and vaccination.

Key Points

  • Vaccines make the body produce its own antibodies.
  • Diet, exercise, hygiene and masks together protect us.

lessons.notes_html:
• Atomic number (Z) — number of protons in the nucleus. Under normal conditions it equals the number of electrons. Example: 10 protons means atomic number 10; fluorine has atomic number 9, so it has 9 protons.

  • An element with atomic number 4 has 4 electrons around its nucleus.

  • Neutrons = A − Z.

lessons.title: Physical and Chemical Properties
lessons.notes_html:
Physical Properties

  • Hardness — ability to withstand scratches and wear: an iron nail scratches plastic; diamond is extremely hard and cuts other materials; graphite is soft and marks paper.
  • Melting point — temperature at which a solid changes into liquid.
  • Boiling point — temperature at which a liquid changes into gas.
  • Solubility — maximum amount of a substance that can dissolve in 100 gram of solvent at a particular temperature and pressure; water is the most common solvent.
  • Thermal conductivity — ability to conduct heat: copper and aluminum (high) are used in heat exchangers, wiring and utensils; wood, polystyrene, wool and plastic (low) are used in insulation and packaging.
  • Electrical conductivity — metals conduct current; copper wire is used in home, school and industry wiring.

Chemical Properties

  • Reactivity — tendency to undergo chemical reactions: baking powder decomposes on heating and produces carbon dioxide, making bakery products porous, soft and fluffy.
  • Flammability — ability to catch fire (burn): acetylene burning with oxygen gives a high-temperature flame for welding and cutting metals.

Ice and vapours: both are H2O — ice is the solid form (freezes at 0°C) and vapours the gaseous form (boils at 100°C or evaporates); they differ in state, not in chemical substance.

Key Points

  • Flammability is chemical; conductivity is physical.
  • Physical changes affect physical properties only.

lessons.title: Combustion and Chemical Equations
lessons.notes_html:
Combustion is a chemical reaction between a fuel and oxygen. Oxygen is essential — it acts as a reactant. During combustion a substance reacts with oxygen.

Burning Methane

  • Reactants: methane (CH4) and oxygen (O2).
  • Products: carbon dioxide (CO2) and water (H2O), along with heat and light.

Chemical Equations

A chemical equation represents a chemical change in symbols, formulae and signs: reactants on the left, products on the right, separated by an arrow towards the products.

  • Sulfur + oxygen: S (s) + O2 (g) → SO2 (g).
  • Zinc + hydrochloric acid: Zn (s) + 2HCl (aq) → ZnCl2 (aq) + H2 (g) — the gas produced is hydrogen.

State symbols: (s) solid, (aq) aqueous, (g) gaseous.

Key Points

  • Combustion always needs oxygen.
  • Zinc with hydrochloric acid gives hydrogen gas.

lessons.title: Rusting, Tarnishing and Acid Rain
lessons.notes_html:
Rusting

Rusting is a chemical process: iron reacts with oxygen and moisture in air to form iron oxide (rust) on the surface. A piece of iron kept in open air for days gets a film of corrosion — iron oxide. Both oxygen and water are needed; dry oxygen alone does not rust iron.

Tarnishing

Tarnishing is a chemical process in which metals like silver, copper or brass react with oxygen and sulfur compounds in air to form a dark, dull layer. Example: silver reacts with hydrogen sulfide (H2S) and oxygen to form silver sulfide (Ag2S) and water — the dark layer on tarnished coins. Tarnish is a thin film of corrosion over copper, brass, magnesium, etc.

Acid Rain Pollutants

The combustion emissions causing smog and acid rain are: sulfur dioxide (SO2), nitric oxide (NO) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs).

Key Points

  • Rust is iron oxide; it needs oxygen plus moisture.
  • Tarnish is a dark sulfide-type film, as on silver coins.

lessons.title: Valency, Ions and Electronic Configuration
lessons.notes_html:
• Valency — the combining capacity of an atom: the number of electrons an atom loses, gains or provides for sharing during combination. Sodium and chlorine: valency 1 each (in NaCl); hydrogen: 1 (in HCl); oxygen: 2 (in H2O); nitrogen: 3 (in NH3); carbon: 4 (in CH4).
  • Electronic configuration — the arrangement of electrons around the nucleus. Atoms tend to get stability by gaining 2 or 8 electrons in the outermost shell like noble gases. Sodium is 2, 8, 1; chlorine is 2, 8, 7; nitrogen has 5 electrons in its valence shell (2, 5); helium (2 in K shell) is stable — He has a stable electronic configuration.

Ions

An ion is the charged particle formed when an atom or group of atoms loses or gains electrons.

FeatureCation (positive ion)Anion (negative ion)
Formed byLosing electron(s)Gaining electron(s)
ExamplesNa+, Mg2+, NH4+Cl-, S2-, OH-
  • A single-atom anion is a simple ion; an ion of more than one atom is a molecular ion — ammonium (NH4+) and hydroxide (OH-) are molecular ions. NH4+ is a cation; S2- is an anion.
  • Sodium has 1 electron in its outermost shell; chlorine has 7; oxygen is a divalent element.

Key Points

  • Lose electrons → cation; gain electrons → anion.
  • Valency: Na 1, O 2, N 3, C 4 in the unit's examples.

lessons.title: Chemical Bonds: Ionic and Covalent
lessons.notes_html:
A chemical bond is the force of attraction that combines atoms together and holds them in a substance. Bonds form in three ways: donating valence electrons, gaining electrons, and mutual sharing of valence electrons.

FeatureIonic bondCovalent bond
How formedComplete transfer of electron(s)Mutual sharing of electrons
ExampleNaCl — sodium loses an electron, chlorine gains itH2, HCl, H2O (single); O2, CO2 (double); N2 (triple)

Types of Covalent Bond

  • Single — one electron pair shared: H2, Cl2, HCl, H2O.
  • Double — two electron pairs shared: O2, CO2.
  • Triple — three electron pairs shared: N2 — the bond between nitrogen atoms is triple covalent.

Two or more atoms combine to form a molecule. One molecule of chlorine gas has 2 atoms.

Honest note on the metallic bond: the exercise asks students to investigate the metallic bond, but Unit 6 teaches only ionic and covalent bonds and never defines the metallic bond. No model answer is given for it here — it is left as a classroom investigation, exactly as in the solved book.

Key Points

  • Transfer makes ionic bonds; sharing makes covalent bonds.
  • N2 has a triple covalent bond.

lessons.title: Solutions, Solute and Solvent
lessons.notes_html:
A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more substances — its colour, density, appearance and other properties are the same in every part.

  • Solute — the part present in less (smaller) quantity, e.g. sugar in sugar solution.
  • Solvent — the part present in more (larger) quantity, e.g. water in sugar solution.

Solute and solvent are the components of a solution. A solution of two substances is a binary solution. Sea water is a solution: water is the solvent and dissolved salts are the solutes, mixed uniformly.

Preparing a Solution

Take a measured amount of solvent and add the solute in small amounts, stirring until it dissolves uniformly — e.g. a teaspoon of sugar stirred into a glass of water. By the particle model, solute particles enter the intermolecular spaces of the solvent and mix homogeneously.

Dissolving Faster

  • Increase the temperature.
  • Stir — fresh solvent meets the solute.
  • Break the solid into smaller pieces — more surface area.

Key Points

  • Less quantity = solute; more quantity = solvent.
  • A solution is uniform in every part.

mcqs.why: Sea water is a solution: water is the solvent and dissolved salts are the solutes, mixed uniformly.

lessons.notes_html:
1. Nature of Solute and Solvent

Like dissolves like: water has ionic character, so ionic compounds like sodium chloride dissolve in water, while covalent compounds dissolve in covalent solvents.

2. Temperature

  • Solubility of sodium chloride, copper sulphate and potassium nitrate increases with temperature. Heating a saturated salt solution lets more salt dissolve.

  • White washing: use cold water for lime, because lime dissolves more in cold water.

3. Pressure

Pressure affects gaseous solutes in liquids: carbon dioxide is dissolved in soda water under pressure; when the cap is opened, pressure is released and the gas bubbles out.

Key Points

  • Most solids dissolve more when heated; gases and lime dissolve less.
  • Pressure matters for gases in liquids.

lessons.title: Force and Its Effects
lessons.notes_html:
Force is a push or pull that we apply on an object. Push and pull make things move or stop or change direction. Friction, gravity, tension and normal force are also examples of force.

Effects of Force

  • Make objects at rest move.
  • Stop moving objects.
  • Change the speed of a moving object.
  • Change the shape of an object.
  • Change the direction of a moving object — so the statement 'force cannot change direction' is not true.

Units to Remember

  • Force — Newton (N), the SI unit of force.
  • 1 N = 1 kg × 1 m/s² — the force that accelerates 1 kg by 1 m/s². Named after Sir Isaac Newton.

Key Points

  • Force is a push or pull with five clear effects.
  • The SI unit of force is the newton.

lessons.title: Speed, Units and Calculations
lessons.notes_html:
Speed is a measure of how fast or slow an object moves per unit time.

Speed (v) = distance (S) / time (t)

SI Units

QuantitySI unitOther units
DistanceMetre (m)Kilometre (km), mile (mi)
TimeSecond (s)Minute (min), hour (h); 1 hr = 60 min
SpeedMetre per second (m/s)Kilometre per hour (km/h)

Worked Examples

  • A person runs 100 m in 20 s: speed = 100 / 20 = 5 m/s.
  • A car covers 1000 m in 10 s with uniform speed: speed = 1000 / 10 = 100 m/s.
  • Average speed of a 12-hour journey: total distance = 90 + 150 + 240 = 480 km; average speed = 480 / 12 = 40 km/h.

Key Points

  • Always divide total distance by total time for average speed.
  • Speed unit comes from distance unit divided by time unit.

lessons.title: Vibrations, Waves and Sound
lessons.notes_html:
The back-and-forth motion of objects is called vibrations. A wave is any disturbance that carries energy through matter or vacuum, without transferring the material itself.

Sound

  • Sound is a form of energy, produced by vibrating objects, travelling in the form of waves.
  • Sound energy is the kinetic energy of vibrating bodies — the energy transferred to the surrounding medium. High sounds have more energy; low sounds have less.
  • Sound is produced by a drum's diaphragm, a tuning fork's prongs, guitar strings and our vocal organs. When we clap, air particles vibrate and waves spread in all directions to our ears.
  • Sound needs a material medium (solid, liquid or gas) to travel. It cannot travel in vacuum — we do not hear explosions on the Sun because of the vacuum between the Sun and the Earth.

Key Points

  • No vibration, no sound.
  • Sound needs a medium; light does not.

  • Frequency (f) — number of complete waves passing a fixed point in one second; measured in hertz (Hz).
  • Time period (T) — time taken for one complete wave to pass a fixed point. T = 1/f and f = 1/T. Example: 50 Hz gives T = 1/50 = 0.02 second.

An echo is the reflection of sound waves off a surface back to the listener's ears — e.g. shouting in a large empty room or against a cliff. An echo is heard clearly when the reflecting surface is 17 metres away and hard; a soft surface like a cushion absorbs sound and does not reflect it.

How Sound Travels in Air

A vibrating diaphragm pushes nearby air particles to make a high-pressure zone (compression), then moves inward to make a low-pressure zone (rarefaction). Alternate compressions and rarefactions move out as sound waves, while air particles only vibrate back and forth.

Key Points

  • Frequency and time period are inverses of each other.
  • Echo needs a hard surface about 17 m away to be heard clearly.

lessons.title: Expansion and Contraction of Matter
lessons.notes_html:
On heating, particle kinetic energy increases, particles push apart and the substance expands. On cooling, kinetic energy decreases, particles come closer and the substance contracts.

StateOn heatingAmount
SolidParticles vibrate more about fixed positionsLeast — usually very small
LiquidParticles move more and spread outMore than solids, less than gases
GasParticles move freely and spread far apartMost — very noticeable

Everyday Effects and Uses

  • Gaps are left after every few metres in railway tracks and concrete roads, and at one end of bridges (on rollers), so expansion in summer does not bend, sag or crack them — tracks can de-track in summer due to expansion.
  • Overhead wires are strung loosely: they sag in summer and become tight (and can snap) in winter.
  • A metal tyre is heated so it expands, fitted over a wooden wheel, then contracts on cooling and grips tightly. A hot rivet contracts on cooling and pulls steel plates together.
  • A heated metal ball does not pass through a ring; after cooling it passes again.
  • Thermometer: mercury or alcohol expands and rises in the tube when hot, and contracts and falls when cold — the rise of mercury level is due to expansion of mercury. This is the main use of expansion and contraction of liquids.
  • Different substances expand at different rates because their particle arrangement, spacing and forces differ. In a sealed steel container, heating a gas raises its pressure (volume and mass stay fixed).

Key Points

  • Expansion order: gases most, then liquids, then solids least.
  • Expansion gaps prevent damage in summer heat.

lessons.notes_html:
Water conservation means saving water. Irrigation technology conserves water and increases agricultural yields.

Drip Irrigation

  • Application of water only to the root zone of plants.
  • Water is delivered directly to the roots through small holes in drip emitters.

  • It is the system used in areas with limited water resources, ensures proper hydration and increases yields.

  • Lemon juice — preservative in apple jam.

lessons.title: Making Pickles and Jam: Procedures
lessons.notes_html:
Mango Pickle

Ingredients: un-ripened mangoes (4–5 pieces), salt, vinegar (preservative), pickle jar with lid — all of these are essential.

  • Wash mangoes and cut into pieces; dry them in the sun.
  • Keep dried pieces dipped in salt water overnight.
  • Put into clean, sterilized jars containing vinegar solution; air-tight the jars.
  • Ready for use in 15 days.

Onion Pickle

Materials: onion, 2 cinnamon sticks, 6 whole cloves, a pinch of crushed red pepper flakes, 1 cup (240 mL) vinegar, 1/2 cup (120 mL) lime juice, 1/2 cup (100 g) sugar, 1 tablespoon common salt. Dip sliced onions in boiled water for 12 minutes, drain into a sterilized jar; heat spices 3–5 minutes, add vinegar, lime juice, sugar and salt until dissolved, pour over onions and close the lid. Ready in about 20 days.

Apple Jam

Ingredients: sliced apple (2 bowls), sugar (1/3 cup), cinnamon (1 small stick), orange zest (1 tablespoon), lemon juice (preservative), and a bottle (jar). Salt is not used in apple jam. Wash apples, remove skin, slice; mix with sugar, cinnamon, orange zest and lemon juice; cook at medium heat until it simmers, then simmer at medium-low for 20 to 30 minutes; store in a jar.

Key Points

A sanitizer is a liquid material used to kill germs. Materials: distilled water, glycerine, isopropyl alcohol, hydrogen peroxide, and a plastic or glass container.

Simple Stethoscope

A stethoscope is a medical device for listening to the heartbeat and counting the pulse rate. Materials: a Y-shaped tube, fine hollow plastic tubes, cotton, a balloon, scissors, insulation tape and a funnel.

  • Fix small hollow tubes over the two upper limbs of the Y-tube; fix cotton swabs on their free ends.

lessons.title: Gravitational Force
lessons.notes_html:
According to Isaac Newton, every object attracts every other object. This force is called gravitational force or gravity — the force of attraction between any two masses.

  • The larger the mass of an object, the stronger the gravitational force it exerts.
  • The closer the two objects are, the stronger the gravitational force between them.
  • The Earth pulls every object towards its centre, and the object also pulls the Earth towards its own centre. Because the Earth's mass is far greater, dropped things move towards the Earth's centre.

Key Points

  • Gravity grows with mass and shrinks with distance.
  • Every pair of masses attracts each other.

lessons.title: Tides and Seasons
lessons.notes_html:
Tides

  • Tides are the rising and falling of sea levels, caused by the gravitational pull of the Moon: the pull is stronger on the side facing the Moon and weaker on the opposite side, so oceans bulge towards and away from the Moon — high tides on both sides, low tides in between. The Sun's gravity and Earth's rotation also play a part.
  • The Moon pulls ocean water more strongly than the Sun because it is closer to the Earth, although the Sun is far more massive.
  • When the Sun and Moon line up with the Earth (new or full Moon), combined pull creates higher spring tides.
  • Low tides help fishermen move forward in the sea; high tides help them come back. Tides used to generate electricity are tidal energy, a renewable source.

Seasons

  • Seasons are caused by the tilt of the Earth (about 23.5°) together with its orbital motion around the Sun. One revolution takes 365 days (one year).
  • Summer solstice — around June 22 in the Northern Hemisphere: North Pole tilted towards the Sun, longest day, summer begins. On 22 June the southern hemisphere has winter.
  • Winter solstice — around December 22 in the Northern Hemisphere: shortest day, winter begins.
  • Spring equinox — around March 21; autumn equinox — around September 23: day and night nearly equal.
  • Seasons are opposite in the two hemispheres: when Pakistan (Northern Hemisphere) has summer, Australia (Southern Hemisphere) has winter.

Key Points

  • Tides come mainly from the Moon's pull; seasons from Earth's tilt plus revolution.

lessons.title: Constellations, Galaxies and Other Stars
lessons.notes_html:
A constellation is a specific pattern or shape formed by a group of stars in the sky — an area of the sky used for reference, so a star is easy to recognise by its constellation.

  • There are 88 constellations covering the whole sky; in old days they were used to set direction for navigation at sea.
  • Famous ones: Ursa Major (Big Dipper / Great Bear) — seven stars, four making the bowl and three the handle, with a bright star at the end of the bowl pointing to the pole star; Leo (seen March to May); Orion.
  • Different constellations appear in different parts of the year because of Earth's revolution: Cygnus and Aquila in northern summer; Orion and Taurus in northern winter.

Directed Study (library / internet, as the book directs)

  • Other stars have planets: yes — astronomers have discovered thousands of planets orbiting other stars, called exoplanets, so planetary systems are not unique to our Sun. (This answer comes from the book's directed library/internet study, not from Unit 12's text.)
  • Galaxy: a huge system of billions of stars with gas and dust, held together by gravity — e.g. our Milky Way. A constellation differs because it is only a pattern as seen from Earth: its stars are not physically bound and may lie at very different distances. A galaxy is a real, physically bound system.

Key Points

  • 88 constellations map the whole sky.
  • A constellation is a seen pattern; a galaxy is a real star system.
